attrs.management_says: No explanation for 2015 receivables or operating cash flow movements is present in the provided MD&A excerpts. The only cash flow discussion (E47) covers 2014 vs 2013.
attrs.numbers_show: Receivables grew 8% ($344.4M → $372.0M) while revenue grew 10.7%; DSO improved 60→58 days annually (E7, E18, E23). But quarterly signals show Q3 receivables +15.5% vs revenue +13.7% (DSO 62→63) and Q4 receivables +8.0% vs revenue +3.3% (DSO 46→48), indicating late-year shipment timing (E27, E28). Operating cash flow fell 49% ($185.8M → $95.1M) while net income rose 27% ($137.2M → $174.3M) (E5, E6, E16, E17, E24).

attrs.reason: The 49% drop in operating cash flow ($185.8M → $95.1M) alongside a 27% rise in net income is not explained by quantified drivers in the pack. Defender cites seasonal inventory build and ERP disruption (E30, E49), but these are qualitative MD&A statements; no reported numbers (e.g., inventory changes, payables, ERP costs) show the size of these effects. Quarterly receivables signals (E27, E28) show a Q3/Q4 surge but do not quantify the cash flow impact.

rebuttal.innocent_explanation: The 49% drop in operating cash flow despite higher net income reflects normal seasonal working capital investment (inventory build for fall shipments) and temporary cash conversion disruption from the May 2015 ERP implementation in international distributor businesses; the Q3/Q4 receivables surge aligns with the disclosed timing of fall season wholesale shipments.
